title: Dying well
hookLine: old Christian handbooks taught the art of dying well

lines: A MAN IN BED, NEAR THE END.
cards: Old woodcuts, in pairs. In the first, a man lies in bed, plainly near the end, and little devils crowd the room, whispering, holding up things to tempt him.
In the next, an angel stands close with an answer, and the devils fall back.
The pictures come from a kind of old Christian handbook, copied, printed and translated, with a two-word Latin title: ars moriendi, the art of dying.
A whole book, written for ordinary people, about the one thing nobody gets to do twice.

teach.h: DYING AS AN ART YOU CAN LEARN.
teach.b: Calling it an art is the surprise. An art is something you learn, practice and get better at. The handbook treats a good death the same way: not as luck, but as something a person can prepare for while still well.
It imagines the deathbed as a last struggle.

The dying person is tempted to doubt their faith, to despair over everything they've done wrong, to grow impatient with pain, to feel proud of their own goodness, and to cling to their money, their things and their people.
For each temptation, an angel in the pictures offers a counter. Against despair, trust in mercy. Against impatience, patience.
Against pride, humility. Against clinging, letting go. It's less a list of rules than a set of turns the heart can make, even at the very end.
The handbook also speaks to whoever sits at the bedside: questions to gently ask, prayers to read aloud, an image of the cross held where the dying person can see it.
Dying well, in these books, was not meant to be done alone.
And they carry a quiet suggestion: don't wait for the deathbed.
The turns can be practiced now, on a day when nothing is wrong.

how: Some Christians prepare for death with prayer, confession, anointing or last rites, and by talking with family and clergy; chaplains and hospice teams may help with what people call a good death.

the art of dying: old handbooks on preparing for a good death

games.q: what's inside the art of dying — tap the pairs.
p: Latin for the art of dying
prayers read, a cross held up

s: the ars moriendi was written only for priests
it was written for ordinary people, and for those at the bedside.
the handbook treats a good death as something you can prepare for
that's why it's called an art.
in the woodcuts, the dying man faces his temptations alone
each temptation picture is followed by one where an angel answers it.

games.q: you're sitting with someone near the end, and they're sinking into despair over their past. what does the old handbook suggest?
o: turn them gently toward trust in mercy.
games.why: against despair, the handbook's angel answers with trust in mercy.

practice: Ask yourself gently, without forcing an answer: what would dying well mean to me?

Maybe it's who is there, what has been said or forgiven, or simply not being afraid; let one sentence form without polishing it, and if nothing comes, that's an answer too. If you pray, you can hold the question before God.

wordCard.voice: Ars moriendi: Latin for the art of dying, the name of old Christian handbooks that taught people how to prepare for a good death. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from late medieval Christian handbooks: the art of dying.

carryVoice: Your line: against clinging, letting go. The old books called it an art because it can be learned. That's day seven hundred eighty.
